text.text: Run the salon from here. Appointments shows the day by stylist; each finished visit records the service price, tip, retail sold and the stylist's commission, and whether the client rebooked before leaving. Client cards keep the color formula, patch test date and hair notes, so any stylist can pick up where the last one left off.
Everything on the menu, its price, time and how many regulars book it.

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the salon runs in this workspace. Share it with the front desk and every stylist.

Change the service menu to your own prices and times, set your commission percentages in the commission formula, and delete the sample clients once you have entered a dozen of your own. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Long color services and bridal parties take a deposit when booking; record it as a payment with method
and take it off the final bill. Gift cards are recorded as payments by gift card, so the day's totals still add up.
The healthiest salons book the next visit before the client leaves the chair. A rebooking rate above 60 percent means a full book; under 40 means the front desk is chasing every week.
When a client calls to book
tell you what to book and with whom.
Book the right length. A partial balayage is three hours, not two; the service menu lists minutes for each service. Under-booking color is the main reason a day runs late.
New color clients: book a 15-minute consultation and a patch test at least 48 hours before the color appointment. Put the date in
Clients with two or more no-shows show
. Take a card deposit when booking.
The stylist suggests the next visit while finishing: "Your roots will show in five to six weeks. Shall I hold the same time on the 14th?"
Cut clients: four to eight weeks. Root touch-ups: four to six. Balayage: ten to fourteen.
Book it before the client reaches the desk, and tick
If they will not commit, mark them
and text them in two weeks.
Service price confirmed with the stylist, extras added (bond repair, toner, extra length)

Next visit booked, or the client marked Due to rebook
Payment taken and Mark paid pressed

A color client finishes her root touch-up. While she is under the dryer, the stylist checks the book and suggests a Tuesday in five weeks. At the desk, the client buys the color-safe shampoo the stylist used. The appointment shows Rebooked, Retail sold $32, and the stylist's commission includes 10 percent of the retail.
Text a reminder two days before and on the morning of the visit. A no-show is set as
on the appointment; the client card counts them. After two, ask for a deposit when they next book. Be kind about the first one: life happens.
The rebooking donut shows the share of finished visits that left with a next appointment. Look at it by stylist at the monthly team meeting; the stylist with the highest rate shares how they ask.
A color formula on the client card is worth more than any stylist's memory. It is what lets another colorist step in when someone is sick, and what protects the salon if a result goes wrong.
What to record after every color service
on the client card, newest first, with the date:
Product line and shades, with the ratio (for example 6N + 6.1, 1 to 1)
Where it went: roots only, all over, mid-lengths, foils, hand-painted
Processing time and whether heat was used
Toner or gloss: shades and time
Result in your own words, and anything you would change next time
Every new color client, and every client whose last color was more than six months ago, gets a patch test 48 hours before color.
. No date, no color: rebook the service.
Any reaction: stop, note it in
Read the formula and notes on the card
Look at the hair in daylight: regrowth length, previous color, porosity
Agree the result with the client, using pictures, and say what is realistic in one visit
Corrections take longer and cost more than the original service. Book a consultation first, price it in writing, and plan more than one visit if needed. Record each step of the formula.

A regular's colorist is out sick. Another colorist opens the client card: 7G + 7N, 20 volume, 35 minutes on the roots, then a 9V gloss for 10 minutes. The client leaves with the same color she always has and does not notice the change of hands.

If a result is not what was agreed, tell the owner the same day. Offer a fix at no charge within a week. Write what happened and what was done on the card. Most clients stay when it is handled quickly and kindly.
Retail is the easiest money in the salon: a client who loves the result wants to keep it at home. Recommend what you used, keep the shelf stocked, and close the day the same way every night.
Recommend one or two products the stylist actually used, and explain why for this client's hair.
Put the bottle in the client's hand at the chair, not at the desk.

on each appointment is 45 percent of the service price plus 10 percent of retail. Change the percentages in the formula to match your own pay plan, and keep tips separate: tips belong to the stylist in full. Add up each stylist's appointments for the pay period from the appointments table.

At the end of a busy Saturday the front desk checks that 22 appointments are marked done, adds up card and cash, and sees that the texture spray is down to four bottles, under the reorder point of five. It goes on Monday's order.
Stylists who are shy about selling usually do better with one question: "Do you want to know what I used today?" It is advice, not a sales pitch.
